title: Part V — TRUST: Keeping the Marketplace Safe
basis: Reconstructed on 2026-11-12 from the published page (posts/part-5-intro/index.md) and its former spec.md (accepted 2026-10-21), which it replaces; one spec paragraph per unit of the page, in the page's order. Intent outcome, AC-1 to AC-3 and role are copied unchanged from the post's entry in journal-spec.json; the introduction realises Part V's opening (hook, bridge, roadmap) from the same file. The journal spec gives this post no thesis, so the thesis and its three supporting claims are written here from the part's thesis and flow. The five callouts (IN THIS PART, WHY THE BUSINESS CARES, WHY ARCHITECTS SHOULD CARE, KEY POINTS, FAILURE PATTERNS) stand before the first paragraph and are kept as the house format; the KEY POINTS callout carries the part's claim in three bullets. know: Part V's argument: trust and safety is a platform capability, not a team with a queue; policy, detection, decision, enforcement and review are joined by one decision record; fraud is caught at its setup by scoring actors and adding friction in proportion to risk; identity is asked for at the moment of risk; regulation asks for a few artifacts built once.
The four chapters in reading order and the question each answers, and the Veldmark incidents and decisions of 2027 they follow.

thesis.question: What does this part argue, and in what order should its chapters be read?
thesis.claim: Part V argues that trust is a platform capability beneath the brands, not a team with a queue per brand: one decision service writes one decision record that every consumer must obey, fraud is caught at its setup by scoring accounts as well as listings and adding friction in proportion to risk, identity is asked for at the moment of risk, and regulation asks for a few artifacts built once, while policy, thresholds and legal grounds stay with each brand; its four chapters are read in the order each plugs into the one before: the platform, the fraud detector that fills its detection slot, the identity checks that detector escalates to, and the regulation that reads the records all three keep.
thesis.disputed_by: The common practice of building trust in the order incidents arrive, as a review queue per brand attached to insertion with fraud, identity and each law handled as separate projects, so the trust chapters are independent topics a reader may consult in any order.
thesis.so_what: A reader who accepts it reads the platform chapter first, or opens the one chapter that answers the trust problem in front of them, and expects every surface built in Parts II to IV, and every revenue line of Part VI, to obey the decisions this platform records.
thesis.how_why: Fraud scoring needs a decision service to turn its scores into enforcement and a propagation path to make them take effect; identity checks are the strongest friction fraud scoring asks for; the law asks for the decision record and trader record the first three chapters build. Veldmark's 2027 incidents failed between stacks: a phishing link reached Femke sixteen minutes after her first buyer contact, and a Barcelona ring of 26 accounts posted 180 fake rentals while its signals sat in separate queues.

Veldmark meets the cost of separate trust stacks in two 2027 incidents and answers with four decisions that the chapters design.

flow.rationale: The page opens on the risk Part IV created (fast discovery is fast for fraudsters too), states the part's claim (trust is one platform with local policy), then gives the reading order with the reason for each chapter's position, and narrows to one row per chapter with the symptom that sends a reader there. It widens once to place the platform in the book, shows Veldmark meeting the cost of separate stacks in two incidents and answering with four decisions, and ends with a short synthesis, the part's test and the hand-off to the first chapter. The order is given before the table because the rows read as a sequence only once the reader knows each chapter builds on the last; the connection section follows the table because it says what the chapters take from Parts II to IV and hand to Part VI; the Veldmark section follows because its incidents are the separate stacks in practice and its decisions are what the chapters design; the conclusion comes last and holds no new material. Put Veldmark first and the incidents arrive before the reader knows which chapter answers each; put the connection first and it names the enforcement overlay and DAC7 before the reader has met the chapters that use them.

evidence.what: On 7 March 2027 a fake Safe Deal payment link reached Femke sixteen minutes after her first buyer contact, and the scammer's phone number had a Motorvane account Tradeyard could not see; in July a Barcelona ring of 26 accounts posted 180 fake rentals and 63 people lost about €71,000 while photo and price signals sat in separate queues. Decisions: Veldmark ID (June 2027), one login across brands with brand profiles, designed so that a sold brand can be cut out; an obligation register mapping the DSA and related rules to controls and evidence queries; a shared trust-and-safety platform live for Tradeyard NL and BE in November 2027 with a cross-brand block list of hashed identifiers; first-contact friction on Tradeyard (December 2027) against scams like Femke's.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md: 'Four of everything'; recurring example 1 (Rotterdam city bike, 19:55 first contact, 20:11 link); recurring example 4 (Barcelona ring); timeline Jun 2027 (Veldmark ID) and Nov 2027 (shared T&S platform); trust-and-safety-architecture T&S baseline line (hashed block list); fraud-prevention first-contact friction line (Dec 2027); marketplace-regulation DSA reporting line (five statement-of-reasons sources); people table (Aisha Rahman, Lucía Ortega).; trust-and-safety-architecture moderator-split line (the suspended account's phone number had also registered a Motorvane private-seller account); fraud-prevention Barcelona ring timeline (hash matches and rent-anomaly flags went to separate queues).
evidence.shows: Both incidents failed between stacks, and each decision joins what the brands kept apart.

conclusion.heading: Where to begin
conclusion.synthesis: Read together, the four chapters build and read the same few records: the decision record, the risk scores that feed it, the identity claims and trader records, and the reports the law asks for; trust is one platform because its records are shared, not because its people are.
conclusion.so_what: Because the records are shared, a fake rental's photo and price signals meet in one record and one decision stops every alert before it reaches a victim, and the group can answer the part's test for any enforcement decision.
